question: How did a reed from India become a word, a medicine and, in some places, a luxury — without yet becoming a food?
summary: This is the longest-lived and best-documented stage of sugar as a rarity. Across nine centuries the folio's evidence shows the same plant seen very differently from three places. In India sugar is a graded family of products, from syrup to white sugar, made with presses and known to farmers, doctors and monks ([[te1]], [[te3]], [[te4]], [[ec4]]). In China it is a southern curiosity, dried in the sun as 'stone honey' and sent north as tribute, with real sugar-making arriving only at the end of the period ([[te2]], [[th6]], [[x3]], [[ec5]]). In Greece and Rome it is a drug, *sakchar*: a solidified honey from India that physicians copy from each other and cooks never use ([[th3]], [[th5]], [[th11]], [[e5]]).

The silences are as telling as the mentions. Alexandria's customs tariff and Diocletian's price edict list oriental spices but not sugar; no Roman recipe sweetens with it ([[o1]], [[o2]], [[e5]]). Persia is where the folio ends: in the sixth century cane is being grown in Khuzestan, around the medical school of Gundeshapur, which becomes the bridge to the next folio ([[th14]], [[p2]], [[p1]]).

So the question this folio answers is not 'when did sugar begin?' but 'how did the idea and the word travel before the product did?' — and the answer is monks, doctors, merchants and one linguistic path from *śarkarā* to *saccharum* ([[x2]]).

themes.title: India: sugar as a graded product
text: The Arthaśāstra's ladder of cane products, the Buddhist 'three boilings' analogy and the medical texts' clones and sugars show that India had an elaborate sugar vocabulary and technology, with the press (mahāyantra, kolhu) and irrigated cane fields. Most of this evidence is Buddhist or medical, which is also why it survives.

themes.title: China: from stone honey to sand sugar
text: Chinese sources move from poems and early botanical notes to a clear regional picture: cane grown in the south, juice dried in the sun, sugar a gift or tribute, and honey and maltose still the sweeteners of the kitchen. By the early sixth century Guangzhou is making a dry 'sand sugar'. Monastic rules and a northern emperor's siege request show cane already prized outside its homeland.

themes.title: The Mediterranean: a drug that never enters the kitchen
text: Dioscorides, Pliny and Galen describe the substance accurately but as medicine; Roman poets pass on the reed-honey as hearsay; and no recipe, tariff or price edict mentions it. Honey and boiled grape must remain the sweeteners the ancient West actually used.

themes.title: Persia: the bridge
text: Persian cane is first noticed in the fifth century, and Sasanian tradition ties it to forced resettlement in Khuzestan and to the physicians of Gundeshapur. The links between these facts are partly legend; that is flagged in the entries.

themes.title: How the word travelled
text: *Śarkarā* ('grit') becomes Pali *sakkharā*, Greek *sákchar* and Latin *saccharum*: the word reaches the Mediterranean centuries before the product is common, which is one reason historians are careful about reading it as sugar.

turning_points.text: Eratosthenes reports that India's large reeds are sweet at the root: the Greek tradition of reed honey continues.
The Arthaśāstra's ladder of cane products shows India already grading sugar by purity.
The Periplus records 'honey from the reed called sacchari' leaving Barygaza for East Africa: the only trade record of cane honey in the period.
Pliny reports saccharon from Arabia and India, used only in medicine.
Diocletian's price edict names oriental spices but not sugar: still too rare to price.
The Armenian Geography places sugarcane at Gundeshapur: the first notice of Persian cane.
'Sand sugar' is made at Guangzhou: a sugar industry of some kind in China.
A Buddhist sutra describes the three boilings from syrup to white sugar.

how_to_read: Start with *Thought*, where most of the written sources live (th1 to th16 are the Greek, Latin, Chinese and Indian authors in rough chronological order), then *Technology* and *Economy* for what people actually did with cane. *Exchange* and *World* give the routes.
The folio is deliberately large because the evidence is scattered; the Overview threads above are the quickest way in. Where an entry's tier is UNVERIFIED, CONTESTED or LEGEND, the note says why.

sources.intro: A mixed evidence base: a handful of ancient texts quoted in translation, but most of the folio rests on modern scholars who have gathered those texts for sugar. The folio is built mainly from five works, none of them an edition of a primary text.
main: Mazumdar, *Sugar and Society in China*, for Chinese textual evidence and the Indian-Chinese comparison (about thirty entries).
Needham, *Science and Civilisation in China* 6.3, with Daniels, for the technology and the Indian record (about twenty entries).
Kieschnick, Laufer, Dalby and Bouras-Vallianatos for the Buddhist, Persian, Greek and Latin strands; Ouerfelli for the Mediterranean reception.
Strabo and the Perseus translations for the few classical passages read directly.
contested: The Mawangdui cane slips are reported but not checked ([[b2]]).
The 'Zhao hun' syrup versus Hawkes's yam sauce ([[e1]]).
Varro Atacinus's line on the Indian reed, which may describe bamboo ([[e3]]).
Patañjali and pseudo-Alexander of Aphrodisias are recorded as sources that exist, not read ([[th2]], [[th7]]).
Khusrau's cane-juice story is told as legend ([[p2]]); the link from Gundeshapur to sugar is inference ([[x4]]).
gaps: No Sanskrit, Pali or Chinese text was read in the original; a specialist reading of the Arthaśāstra, the Vinaya commentaries and the Chinese botanical notes would firm up several dates.
Deerr's *The History of Sugar* and the Arabic sources, which are the other standard accounts of the Persian stage, were not used here.
